posts.angle: Replace piece-count shopping with a finished-dimension fit check
posts.headline: Never buy a puzzle board from piece count alone
posts.copy: A 1000-piece label does not prove fit. Check the finished width and height on two real puzzle boxes, then compare that rectangle with the board's usable area—not its outside dimensions.
posts.assetBrief: Original vertical measuring diagram with two generic puzzle boxes, finished-image arrows, a usable-board rectangle, and no brand logos or merchant imagery.
posts.altText: Checklist comparing a puzzle's finished width and height with a puzzle board's usable interior area.

posts.angle: Make the named storage location the thoughtfulness test
posts.headline: The puzzle-board question that matters tonight
posts.copy: Where will the closed puzzle and sorted pieces live tonight? Name the flat case location, measure the route, reserve a tray shelf, and check the lift. If those answers are vague, the gift is still clutter.
posts.assetBrief: Five original illustrated slides: shared table, tape measure, flat under-bed outline, level tray shelf, and a final buy-or-skip decision; no product photography.
posts.altText: Carousel showing a puzzle case measured for flat under-bed storage and a sorting-tray stack assigned to a shelf.

posts.angle: Separate preserving the image from preserving sorting decisions
posts.headline: A paused puzzle has two kinds of progress
posts.copy: The fitted case protects the assembled image. The tray stack protects the edge, color, and pattern groups that make tomorrow's restart easy. A thoughtful pair keeps both—without taking over the room.
posts.assetBrief: Original two-column diagram labeled Image progress and Sorting progress, converging on a clean shared table; use generic puzzle shapes only.
posts.altText: Diagram showing an unfinished puzzle in a closed flat case beside sorted pieces in a level lidded stack.

posts.angle: Choose the tray companion by closure, contrast, and reach
posts.headline: Lidded stack or shallow trays? Ask three questions
posts.copy: Choose seven colored trays with a top lid when compact closed storage matters. Choose six shallow blue trays when easy scanning and reach matter more. In both cases, check contrast—and remember that neither stack is spill-proof.
posts.assetBrief: Original decision tree comparing a generic lidded colored stack with six shallow blue trays across lid, contrast, reach, and shelf behavior.
posts.altText: Decision tree comparing a top-lidded colored tray stack with shallow blue sorting trays for puzzle pieces.

posts.angle: Challenge vague portability with a flat-storage reality check
posts.headline: Portable does not automatically mean vertical storage
posts.copy: Hook: a handle is not permission to stand every unfinished puzzle on edge. Show the finished-size check, the case weight, and owner-reported loose-piece shift. End with the conservative rule: move carefully, then store flat in a measured place.
posts.assetBrief: Original unbranded storyboard: generic case handle, weight icon, pieces sliding toward an edge, and a final flat under-sofa placement; no simulated product test.
posts.altText: Short video storyboard explaining why a large puzzle case should be measured and stored flat despite portability language.

posts.angle: Make the anchor-only and skip choices as visible as the bundle
posts.headline: When this puzzle pair should be one gift—or none
posts.copy: Buy only the case if its included boards already sort enough. Buy only trays if a fitted storage surface already exists. Skip both when no flat location is named, the lift is uncomfortable, or another system already works.
posts.assetBrief: Original three-column card labeled Pair, One item, and Skip, with generic case and tray line icons plus dimension, storage, and duplicate checks.
posts.altText: Gift decision card showing when to buy a puzzle case and trays together, when to buy one item, and when to skip both.
